meta.title: Who really said "We must be willing to let go of the life we have planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Joseph Campbell did say it - but as "get rid of the life we've planned" (A Joseph Campbell Companion, 1991). The E. M. Forster credit is spurious.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We must be willing to let go of the life we have planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us'?
meta.ogDescription: Right author, wrong words. Campbell's documented line says "get rid of," not "let go of" - and E. M. Forster never wrote it at all.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Correctly credited to Joseph Campbell — but not in these words. What is actually documented in print is “We must be willing to get rid of the life we’ve planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us,” recorded by Diane K. Osbon and published in A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (HarperCollins, 1991); the widely shared “let go of the life we have planned” form is a later smoothing that no primary source pins to Campbell.
answer.confidenceText: Right author, drifted wording — the circulating sentence is a later paraphrase of a documented Campbell line.

source.excerpt: We must be willing to get rid of the life we’ve planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us. The old skin has to be shed before the new one can come.
trail: 1991 — The sentence reaches print in A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living, selected and edited by Diane K. Osbon from what she described as favorite expressions of Campbell’s recorded in her journals. The Internet Archive catalog record ↗ describes the book as Campbell’s words from his Esalen Institute lectures.

1998–2000 — The saying enters newspapers. Quote Investigator ↗ records a December 1998 Anniston Star item using a “let go” rewording with no author attached, and a February 2000 Asbury Park Press piece crediting Campbell with the original “get rid of” phrasing.
2002 — The E. M. Forster credit appears, in Michael Gurian’s The Soul of the Child and in the Orem-Geneva Times of 20 March. QI finds no basis for it ↗ and calls the linkage spurious.
Today — Both the Campbell credit and the smoothed “let go of” wording circulate together. Wikiquote ↗ lists only the “get rid of” form, cited to p. 18 of the 1991 book.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording as printed in the 1991 book, quoted by Quote Investigator ↗ and cited independently by Wikiquote ↗ at p. 18. Note “get rid of,” not “let go of.”

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.heading: About Joseph Campbell
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American writer and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College; comparative mythology
author.bio: Joseph John Campbell (1904–1987) was an American writer and scholar of comparative mythology and comparative religion who taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College for most of his career. He is best known for The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), the Masks of God series, and the posthumous television conversations with Bill Moyers published as The Power of Myth (1988) — and for two ideas that escaped academia entirely: the monomyth, or hero’s journey, and the maxim “follow your bliss.” Much of the aphoristic Campbell that circulates online comes not from his books but from transcriptions of his spoken teaching, which is exactly how this sentence reached print.

misattribution.heading: Two things go wrong with this quote
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case: the famous name on the card is the correct one. What has gone wrong is the wording — and, for two decades, a second author’s name attached to it entirely.

items.why: Forster is credited with the line in Michael Gurian’s The Soul of the Child (2002) and in the Orem-Geneva Times of 20 March 2002 — the earliest Forster credits Quote Investigator ↗ could find. Forster died in 1970, and QI found no support for the attribution in his writings, concluding that “the linkage to E. M. Forster appears to be spurious.”

The sentence as printed reads “We must be willing to get rid of the life we’ve planned” — see Wikiquote’s citation to p. 18 ↗ of the 1991 Companion. The gentler “let go of the life we have planned” appears in newspapers from December 1998, at first with no author attached at all.

The line is not from The Hero with a Thousand Faces or The Power of Myth, as it is sometimes captioned. It reached print in a posthumous compilation of his Esalen Institute lectures ↗, assembled from an editor’s journals four years after his death.

misattribution.truthLine: The person is right; the words drifted. Campbell’s line, as recorded by Diane K. Osbon and published in 1991, is “We must be willing to get rid of the life we’ve planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us” — per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why the line travels so well
lead: Campbell spent a career arguing that myths are instructions for living, and that the hero’s journey always begins with a departure — leaving the known arrangement before the new one is visible. This sentence is that whole argument compressed into one line, which is why it turns up on graduation cards, redundancy notices and mid‑life pep talks far more often than it turns up in Campbell’s actual books.

The reason it is hard to source is that Campbell did not write it for publication. The Internet Archive’s catalog record for the 1991 book describes its contents as “Words of Joseph Campbell from his Esalen Institute lectures ↗,” assembled by Diane K. Osbon from what she called favorite expressions of his recorded in her journals. Spoken lines transcribed years later are exactly the kind of text that drifts.
context.detailsSummary: How “get rid of” became “let go of”
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the drift happening in the press rather than in print. A December 1998 item in The Anniston Star carried an unattributed “We must let go of the life we planned so as to accept the life that is waiting for us.” A February 2000 piece in the Asbury Park Press credited Campbell using the original “get rid of” phrasing. By October 2014 The Morning Call was crediting Campbell with a “let go” version.

“Get rid of” is blunt and a little unlovely; “let go of” is gentler and scans better on a card. That is almost always the direction quotes travel — toward the smoother sentence — which is why a wording that sounds too polished is worth checking.
context.pull: The old skin has to be shed before the new one can come.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this saying, identified its earliest documented appearance as Diane K. Osbon's 1991 compilation A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (HarperCollins, quote pages 8 and 18), reported the printed wording as "We must be willing to get rid of the life we've planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us. The old skin has to be shed before the new one can come," documented later instances (Anniston Star 27 Dec 1998 unattributed; Asbury Park Press 27 Feb 2000 crediting Campbell; Michael Gurian's The Soul of the Child and the Orem-Geneva Times 20 Mar 2002 crediting E. M. Forster; The Morning Call 15 Oct 2014 crediting Campbell with a 'let go' variant), noted Forster died in 1970, and concluded that "the linkage to E. M. Forster appears to be spurious."

Wikiquote's Joseph Campbell page lists "We must be willing to get rid of the life we've planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us" among his quotes, cited to A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (1991), p. 18, and gives his life dates as 26 March 1904 - 30 October 1987. The popularly circulated 'let go of the life we have planned' wording does not appear there.

The Internet Archive catalog record for A Joseph Campbell companion: reflections on the art of living lists Joseph Campbell (1904-1987) as author, Diane K. Osbon as editor, HarperCollinsPublishers New York, 1991, 311 pages, and describes the contents as "Words of Joseph Campbell from his Esalen Institute lectures supplemented by relevant excerpts from his past writings and the writings of others."
Open Library's work record confirms A Joseph Campbell companion: reflections on the art of living, by Joseph Campbell, first published 1991, publisher HarperCollins.

Wikipedia states Joseph John Campbell (26 March 1904 - 30 October 1987) was an American writer and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College working in comparative mythology and comparative religion, known for The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), The Masks of God series, The Power of Myth (1988) with Bill Moyers, the monomyth, and 'follow your bliss'; the article also references A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (1991).
The Joseph Campbell Foundation is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to preserving and sharing the work of Joseph Campbell, distributing his lectures and writings as books, audio, e-books and podcasts.
